title: Getting started
description: What routiva is, the ideas behind it, and a working server in under a minute.
text: What is routiva? # routiva is a small web framework for Node.js that gives you the ergonomics of Express — routing, middleware, request/response helpers, body parsing, static files, CORS, compression, logging and rate limiting — while staying completely dependency-free. Everything is built on Node's own node:http . There is no path-to-regexp , no body-parser , no mime-types , no transitive tree of packages to audit. The whole framework is roughly 1,900 lines across 14 ES modules . bash Copy npm install routiva Requires Node.js 18 or newer . No runtime dependencies. No dev dependencies. routiva is not trying to replace Express for everyone. It is for the projects that want a framework small enough to read end to end, and a dependency graph that is exactly node_modules/routiva . Why another framework? # Express is excellent, mature and battle-tested. But it carries a large transitive dependency tree and a handful of sharp edges that this project smooths over: Async errors were an afterthought. In Express 4, a rejected promise in a handler hangs the request unless you call next(err) yourself. routiva catches rejected promises and thrown errors automatically. The framework is spread across packages. CORS, compression, rate limiting and MIME types each live in their own dependency. routiva ships them in the core. HTTP correctness is optional. Express returns 404 for a path that exists with the wrong method. routiva answers 405 with an Allow header, and handles OPTIONS and HEAD for you. You cannot read it. Express is many files of which the interesting logic is a fraction. routiva is small enough to understand in an afternoon. The mental model # An app is a router . A router is an ordered list of layers . A layer is either a route, a piece of middleware, or an error handler. Requests walk the list top to bottom; the first layer that sends a response ends the journey. text Copy incoming request │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ layer 0 logger() → logs, calls next() │ │ layer 1 cors() → headers, calls next() │ │ layer 2 json() → parses body, next() │ │ layer 3 GET /users/:id → sends a response ────┼──▶ done │ layer 4 error handler → only runs on next(err)│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ That is the entire design. Once you understand the stack, every other page in these docs is detail. Your first server # Create server.js : js Copy import { createApp } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); app. get ( '/' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ hello: 'world' }); }); app. get ( '/users/:id' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ id: req. params . id }); }); app. listen ( 3000 , () => { console. log ( 'listening on http://localhost:3000' ); }); Run it with node server.js (your package.json should have "type": "module" ), then: bash Copy curl http://localhost: 3000 / curl http://localhost: 3000 /users/ 42 Where to go next # If you want to… Read Install it properly and try the bundled demo Installation Build a small app step by step Quick start Understand routes, params and wildcards Routing Learn the middleware stack Middleware Look up a method or option API reference Requirements and compatibility # Requirement Detail Node.js 18.0.0 or newer (uses global fetch in tests, node:test ) Module system ESM. Set "type": "module" or use .mjs Runtime dependencies none TypeScript Ships as plain JavaScript; works with allowJs

title: Installation
description: Install routiva from npm, verify your runtime, and run the bundled demo and test suite.
text: Requirements # routiva runs on Node.js 18 or newer and ships as pure ESM. There is no compiler, bundler or transpile step. Requirement Detail Node.js 18.0.0 or newer ( "engines": { "node": ">=18" } ) Module system ESM — set "type": "module" , or use .mjs files Runtime dependencies none Dev dependencies none Build step none If your project is CommonJS, add "type": "module" to its package.json and switch require calls to import . routiva ships no CommonJS build. Install # bash Copy npm install routiva That installs exactly one package. routiva declares no dependencies and no devDependencies , so the install tree is just node_modules/routiva . Named exports and the default export # The package has one entry point ( src/index.js ) with both named and default exports. Named exports give you the whole toolkit in one import: js Copy import { createApp, Router, HttpError, json, serveStatic } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); The default export is the App class. createApp(options) is simply new App(options) : js Copy import App from 'routiva' ; const app = new App (); The middleware factories are also attached to the class as statics ( App.json() , App.logger() , App.serveStatic() , App.rateLimit() , and so on), so this works too: js Copy import { App } from 'routiva' ; app. use (App. logger ()); app. use (App. json ()); Print the full export list to confirm what is available: bash Copy node -e "import('routiva').then(m => console.log(Object.keys(m).sort().join(' ')))" Verify your setup # Create server.js : js Copy import { createApp } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); app. get ( '/' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ status: 'ok' , node: process. version }); }); app. listen ( 3000 , () => console. log ( 'http://localhost:3000' )); bash Copy node server.js curl http://localhost: 3000 / You should get back {"status":"ok","node":"v18.x.x"} (your version may differ). If that prints, routing, JSON responses and the HTTP server all work. Zero dependencies # No runtime dependencies and no dev dependencies. The test suite is built on node:test and the global fetch , so nothing is installed to run or verify the project. text Copy $ npm ls --all routiva@0.1.2 └── (empty) That also means faster installs, smaller container images, and a supply-chain surface of exactly one package. Run the tests # From a clone of the repository: bash Copy node --test # or: npm test npm run test:watch # re-run on change The suite is 16 test files and 78 tests covering routing, params, request and response APIs, middleware ordering, error propagation, body parsing, cookies, content negotiation, static files, CORS, compression, rate limiting and logging. It starts real HTTP servers on ephemeral ports and makes real requests — there are no mocks. Run the bundled demo # The repository ships a complete CRUD app you can run against the source: bash Copy npm run crud # node crud-app/server.js It listens on port 3000 and serves a browser UI at <http://127.0.0.1:3000> plus a JSON API at /api/products . Override the defaults with environment variables: bash Copy PORT = 4000 HOST = 0.0 . 0.0 DATA_FILE =./tmp/products.json npm run crud Variable Default Purpose PORT 3000 Listening port HOST 127.0.0.1 Listening host DATA_FILE crud-app/data/products.json JSON file used as the datastore Run the app's integration tests on their own: bash Copy npm run crud:test # node --test crud-app/test/crud.test.js npm run crud:smoke # bash crud-app/curl.sh — end-to-end curl script npm run example runs the smaller examples/basic.js demo instead. TypeScript # routiva ships as plain JavaScript with no bundled type declarations and no .d.ts files. With "allowJs": true in your tsconfig.json , TypeScript will import it and infer what it can from the source. Expect some any — there are no generated types yet. No build step # package.json points main and exports straight at src/index.js . There is no dist/ , no bundler config and no prepare script: the code you import is the code in the repository. Where to go next # If you want to… Read Build a small app step by step Quick start Understand the layer stack Core concepts Look up a method or option API reference

title: Quick start
description: Build a small routiva app step by step, then exercise every endpoint with curl.
text: What we are building # One file with a JSON API, request logging, body parsing, a static public/ folder and error handling. Each step adds one piece and explains why. The finished server is about 40 lines. 1. Scaffold the project # bash Copy mkdir routiva -app cd routiva -app npm init -y npm pkg set type=module npm install routiva npm pkg set type=module writes "type": "module" into package.json , which is required — routiva is ESM-only. 2. Your first route # Create server.js : js Copy import { createApp } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); app. get ( '/' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ hello: 'world' }); }); app. listen ( 3000 , () => console. log ( 'http://localhost:3000' )); Run node server.js and open <http://localhost:3000/>. res.json() sets Content-Type: application/json and serializes the object. 3. Add logging and JSON parsing # logger() prints one line per request; json() parses JSON bodies into req.body . Register both before your routes: js Copy import { createApp, logger, json } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); app. use ( logger ()); app. use ( json ()); Both call next() , so the request continues to the routes below. Middleware registered after a route cannot run before it — registration order is execution order. 4. Add a parameterized route # js Copy app. get ( '/users/:id' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ id: req. params . id }); }); :id matches a single path segment. /users/42 sets req.params.id to the string '42' ; /users/42/posts does not match. 5. Read the query string # js Copy app. get ( '/search' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ q: req. query . q , tags: req. query . tag }); }); req.query is parsed from the URL. Repeated keys become arrays, so ?tag=a&tag=b yields { tag: ['a', 'b'] } . 6. Accept a JSON body # js Copy app. post ( '/users' , (req, res) => { res. status ( 201 ). json ({ created: req. body }); }); req.body is populated by json() for application/json requests. Bodies over the 1mb default limit get a 413 ; malformed JSON gets a 400 . 7. Throw an error # Handlers can throw, and async handlers can reject. Either way the error flows to an error handler. routiva has a default one, but a custom handler is easy to add — four parameters marks it, and it is registered last: js Copy import { HttpError } from 'routiva' ; app. get ( '/boom' , async () => { throw new HttpError ( 503 , 'service unavailable' ); }); app. use ((err, req, res, next) => { res. status (err. status || 500 ). json ({ error: { message: err. message } }); }); Without the custom handler, routiva returns { "error": { "message": "...", "status": ... } } for an HttpError and a generic 500 for anything else. 8. Serve a folder of static files # Create public/index.html : html Copy <!doctype html > <html lang = "en" > <head > <meta charset = "utf-8" > <title > routiva </title > </head > <body > <h1 > Served by routiva </h1 > </body > </html > Register the middleware after your routes so an explicit route always wins: js Copy import { serveStatic } from 'routiva' ; app. use ( serveStatic ( 'public' )); serveStatic streams files, sets ETag / Last-Modified for 304 responses, honours single Range requests, and falls through to the next layer when a file is missing. 9. The complete server # js Copy import { createApp, logger, json, serveStatic, HttpError } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); // middleware every request passes through app. use ( logger ()); app. use ( json ()); // routes app. get ( '/' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ hello: 'world' }); }); app. get ( '/users/:id' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ id: req. params . id }); }); app. get ( '/search' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ q: req. query . q , tags: req. query . tag }); }); app. post ( '/users' , (req, res) => { res. status ( 201 ). json ({ created: req. body }); }); app. get ( '/boom' , async () => { throw new HttpError ( 503 , 'service unavailable' ); }); // static files fall back for anything the routes did not match app. use ( serveStatic ( 'public' )); // error handler goes last app. use ((err, req, res, next) => { res. status (err. status || 500 ). json ({ error: { message: err. message } }); }); app. listen ( 3000 , () => console. log ( 'http://localhost:3000' )); 10. Run it and test every endpoint # Start it with node server.js , then run: bash Copy curl http://localhost: 3000 / curl http://localhost: 3000 /users/ 42 curl "http://localhost:3000/search?q=cats&tag=a&tag=b" curl -i -X POST http://localhost: 3000 /users \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"name":"Ada"}' curl -i http://localhost: 3000 /boom curl -i http://localhost: 3000 /index.html What to expect: Request Response GET / {"hello":"world"} GET /users/42 {"id":"42"} GET /search?q=cats&tag=a&tag=b {"q":"cats","tags":["a","b"]} POST /users 201 and {"created":{"name":"Ada"}} GET /boom 503 and {"error":{"message":"service unavailable"}} GET /index.html the HTML file as text/html GET /missing falls through the static middleware to routiva's default 404 JSON. Next steps # Routing — parameters, wildcards, mounted routers and router.route . Middleware — write your own and understand the stack. Error handling — HttpError , error middleware and safe defaults.

title: Core concepts
description: The mental model behind routiva: the layer stack, next(), the raw wrappers, async errors and app settings.
text: The mental model # An app is a router. A router is an ordered list of layers. A layer is a route, a piece of middleware, or an error handler. A request walks the list from top to bottom; each layer either responds, passes control with next() , or signals a failure with next(err) . text Copy createApp() ─▶ App (extends Router) │ └─ stack: [ layer, layer, layer, … ] │ request ────────────▶ walk top to bottom ─▶ first response wins App extends Router # App is a Router with an HTTP server, settings and default responses added. From src/app.js : js Copy export class App extends Router { constructor (options = {}) { super (); this . settings = Object. create ( null ); this . set ( 'env' , options. env || process. env . NODE_ENV || 'development' ); // ... } } Every routing method — get , post , use , param , route — is defined on Router , so an app has them all. A Router on its own is the building block for modular sub-routers: js Copy import { Router } from 'routiva' ; const api = new Router (); api. get ( '/status' , (req, res) => res. json ({ ok: true })); app. use ( '/api' , api); // mounted at a prefix Everything is a layer # Registering a handler pushes one object onto this.stack . A route with three handlers pushes three layers. The shape, from src/router.js : js Copy this . stack . push ({ method, // 'GET' | null (middleware / all) path, // original pattern, for debugging regex, // compiled matcher, built once keys, // captured parameter names fn: handler, // the function actually invoked owner: this , // which Router registered it isMiddleware, // prefix match vs exact match isErrorHandler: handler. length === 4 , }); Routes and middleware share the same array. There is no separate "middleware phase" and "route phase" — only the order you registered things in. Paths are compiled to a RegExp once, at registration, and reused for every request. next() and next(err) # A handler that does not respond must call next() . Calling next(err) switches the stack into error mode. dispatch() enforces the switch with one comparison ( src/router.js , abridged): js Copy function dispatch (stack, req, res, done) { let index = 0 ; let finished = false ; function next (err) { if (finished) return ; // done() runs once if (index >= stack. length ) { finished = true ; return done (err); } const wantsError = Boolean (err); let layer, match; while (index < stack. length ) { layer = stack[index++]; if (layer. isErrorHandler !== wantsError) continue ; // 4-arity ⇔ error mode match = layer. regex . exec (req. path ); if (!match) continue ; if (! methodAllows (layer, req)) continue ; // HEAD→GET, 405 break ; } if (!match) { finished = true ; return done (err); } invoke (layer, match, err, req, res, next); } next (); } A shared cursor means next() from any depth walks forward through the same list without re-running earlier layers. The finished latch guarantees done runs once even if a handler calls next() twice. Registration order is execution order # A use() written before your routes runs first. An error handler written after your routes can catch their errors; one written before them cannot, because it has already been passed. js Copy app. use ( logger ()); // runs first app. get ( '/users' , listUsers); // runs next app. use ((err, req, res, next) => { // runs only if a later layer calls next(err) res. status (err. status || 500 ). json ({ error: { message: err. message } }); }); Error handlers are arity 4 # The only rule is the function's length . Four parameters marks an error handler; three marks an ordinary handler or middleware. No registration API is needed. js Copy app. use ((req, res, next) => { /* normal */ }); // length === 3 app. use ((err, req, res, next) => { /* error */ }); // length === 4 If no error handler responds, App._handleError builds a JSON error. HttpError sets expose = status < 500 , so 4xx messages reach the client while 5xx messages are hidden unless expose stack is on: js Copy const expose = this . setting ( 'expose stack' ); const message = error. expose || expose ? error. message : statusMessage (status); res. status (status). json ({ error: { message, status } }); Request and Response are thin wrappers # Node's IncomingMessage and ServerResponse are wrapped once per request. Both originals stay reachable as req.raw and res.raw , so the framework never hides the socket — anything the wrapper does not cover ( req.raw.setTimeout , res.raw.writeHead ) is still one property away. Request parses the URL, query, cookies and client IP in its constructor, so per-request work happens once. Response makes every mutator chainable ( res.status(201).type('json').send({ ok: true }) ) and guards against a second send by checking res.raw.headersSent || res.raw.writableEnded . Async handlers # Handlers may return a promise. routiva attaches .catch(next) to every returned promise ( src/router.js ), so a rejection is forwarded to the error chain exactly like a synchronous throw — no wrapper library needed: js Copy app. get ( '/data' , async (req, res) => { const row = await db. get (req. params . id ); // rejection reaches your error handler res. json (row); }); This matches Express 5 behaviour. Express 4 only forwarded synchronous throws. Settings # App stores settings on a null-prototype object. Read them with app.setting(key) , write with app.set(key, value) or the boolean helpers app.enable(key) / app.disable(key) . Constructor options set the same keys up front. Setting Default Effect env process.env.NODE_ENV or 'development' Environment name trust proxy false req.ip / req.ips read X-Forwarded-For x-powered-by false Adds X-Powered-By: routiva to responses json spaces 0 Reserved expose stack env !== 'production' 5xx messages and stack traces in error responses js Copy const app = createApp ({ trustProxy: true , xPoweredBy: false }); app. disable ( 'x-powered-by' ); app. set ( 'json spaces' , 2 ); trust proxy also accepts a number: with n , req.ip is taken n hops from the right of X-Forwarded-F

title: Routing
description: Define routes, capture :params and * wildcards, mount sub-routers, and understand exactly how a path is matched.
text: The route methods # Every HTTP method has a matching method on the app (and on a Router ): js Copy import { createApp } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); app. get ( '/users' , (req, res) => res. json ([])); app. post ( '/users' , (req, res) => res. status ( 201 ). json (req. body )); app. put ( '/users/:id' , replaceUser); app. patch ( '/users/:id' , patchUser); app. delete ( '/users/:id' , deleteUser); app. head ( '/users/:id' , headUser); app. options ( '/users/:id' , optionsUser); app. all ( '/ping' , (req, res) => res. send ( 'pong' )); Method Registers get post put patch delete head options A route for that one method all A route for every method (stored with a null method) use Middleware (see Middleware ) A route only runs when both the path and the method match. HEAD is special: it is served by a matching GET route, with the body suppressed. See HEAD, OPTIONS and 405 . More than one handler per route # Any number of handlers can be registered for one path. Each becomes its own layer sharing the same compiled pattern, so they run in order: js Copy app. get ( '/reports/:id' , requireAuth, loadReport, (req, res) => { res. json (req. report ); }); requireAuth runs first, calls next() to continue, then loadReport , then the final handler. Arrays are flattened, so app.get('/x', [a, b], c) works too. This is the same trick Express uses for route-level middleware. Path parameters # A :name segment captures one path segment (everything up to the next / ): js Copy app. get ( '/users/:id' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ id: req. params . id }); }); Pattern Request Match? req.params /users/:id /users/42 ✅ { id: '42' } /users/:id /users/42/ ✅ { id: '42' } (trailing slash tolerated) /users/:id /users/42/posts ❌ — /users/:id /users/a%20b ✅ { id: 'a b' } (decoded) /users/:id/posts/:postId /users/7/posts/9 ✅ { id: '7', postId: '9' } Captured values are URL-decoded with a safe wrapper, so a malformed escape such as %E0%A4 is left as-is instead of throwing a 500 . Params from an outer layer and an inner layer are merged , with the inner value winning. When a mounted router matches :tenant and a route inside it matches :id , the handler sees both. text Copy app.use('/t/:tenant', router) // captures { tenant } router.get('/u/:id', handler) // captures { id } // handler sees { tenant, id } routiva supports required :name segments only. Optional ( :id? ), inline regex ( :id(\\d+) ) and arrays of paths are not part of the syntax — validate inside a param() callback or the handler instead. Wildcards # * captures the rest of the path (including slashes) under the key wildcard : js Copy app. get ( '/files/*' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ path: req. params . wildcard }); }); Pattern Request req.params.wildcard /files/* /files/a/b/c.txt 'a/b/c.txt' /files/* /files/ '' * /anything/at/all 'anything/at/all' A bare * route is the usual single-page-app or catch-all fallback, and is matched with the lowest priority because it is registered last: js Copy app. get ( '*' , (req, res) => res. sendFile ( 'dist/index.html' )); How a path is compiled # Patterns are compiled to a RegExp once, at registration , and reused for every request. compile(pattern, end) in src/router.js normalises the leading and trailing slashes, splits on :name and * , regex-escapes the literals, and turns :name into ([^/]+) and * into (.*) . text Copy /users/:id end → /^\/users\/([^/]+)\/?$/ exact /files/* end → /^\/files\/(.*)\/?$/ exact /api (mount) end → /^\/api(?=\/|$)/ prefix / end → /^\/?$/ prefix → /^/ Two details matter: Routes use an exact match that tolerates a trailing slash ( ^…/?$ ). Mounted middleware uses a prefix match with a lookahead ( ^…(?=/|$) ), so /api matches /api and /api/users but not /apis . Matching is case-sensitive : /Users and /users are different paths. The captured names are stored in a keys array alongside the regex, and zipped back onto the match at request time, so parameter order is preserved. Mounted routers # A Router is a self-contained stack you can mount on a path: js Copy import { App, Router } from 'routiva' ; const api = new Router (); api. get ( '/status' , (req, res) => res. json ({ status: 'ok' })); const app = new App (); app. use ( '/api' , api); app.use('/api', api) mounts the router at the /api prefix. When a request reaches it, the prefix is stripped before the inner router runs, so the router above sees /status , not /api/status — exactly like an Express sub-app. The original req.path , req.url , req.params and req.route are saved and restored the moment the mounted layer calls next() , so an outer route can continue where the inner router left off. Routers nest: mount a router inside a router, and each prefix is stripped and restored in turn. js Copy const admin = new Router (); admin. get ( '/users' , (req, res) => res. json ({ scope: 'admin' })); const v1 = new Router (); v1. use ( '/admin' , admin); // /v1/admin/users app. use ( '/v1' , v1); router.route() # Register several methods for one path with a chainable builder: js Copy app. route ( '/items' ) . get (listItems) . post (createItem) . delete (clearItems); The chain exposes get , post , put , patch , delete , head , options and all , and every call returns the chain so calls can be stacked. router.param() # param(name, fn) registers a callback that runs whenever name appears in a matched route's parameters, before that route's handlers: js Copy import { HttpError } from 'routiva' ; app. param ( 'id' , (req, res, next, id, name) => { if (!/^\d+$/. test (id)) { return next ( new HttpError ( 400 , `${name} must be numeric` )); } req. userId = Number (id); next (); }); app. get ( '/users/:id' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ id: req. userId }); // already validated and coerced }); Argument Meaning req , res The wrapped request and response next Continue to the route handler, or next(err) to fail value The decoded parameter value name The parameter name Callbacks are looked up on the router that registered the route, so a mounted r

title: Middleware
description: What a middleware function is, how ordering works, how to mount routers and paths, and how to write your own.
text: What middleware is # Middleware is a function with three parameters: js Copy function middleware (req, res, next) { // read the request, set headers, maybe respond … next (); // … then pass control down the stack } A middleware either ends the request by sending a response, or passes it on with next() . It can also fail the request with next(err) , which switches the stack into error mode. Anything registered with app.use() is middleware; a route handler is just middleware that also has to match a method. Registering middleware # js Copy import { createApp, logger, cors, json } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); app. use ( logger ()); // every request app. use ( cors ()); app. use ( json ()); app. get ( '/health' , (req, res) => res. json ({ status: 'ok' })); app.use(fn) runs on every request that reaches it, regardless of path. Passing an array works too: app.use([logger(), cors()]) . Mounting under a path # Give use() a path to run the middleware only for that prefix: js Copy app. use ( '/api' , requireApiKey); // /api, /api/users, /api/users/42, … app. use ( '/admin' , adminOnly); // not /adminx The prefix match uses a lookahead, so /api matches /api and /api/users but not /apis . When the middleware runs, the mount prefix is stripped from req.path and req.url , and everything is restored on next() — the same mechanism mounted routers use (see Routing ). js Copy app. use ( '/api' , (req, res, next) => { console. log (req. path ); // "/users" for a request to /api/users next (); // after this, req.path is "/api/users" again }); A path can be given without handlers only if you pass at least one function; app.use('/api') with no handler throws a TypeError . Ordering # There is one stack , and registration order is execution order . This is the whole mental model: js Copy app. use ( logger ()); // 1 app. use ( json ()); // 2 app. get ( '/users' , listUsers); // 3 ← responds app. use ((err, req, res, next) => { // 4 ← only on next(err) res. status ( 500 ). json ({ error: { message: err. message } }); }); Consequences worth internalising: Middleware registered after a route cannot run before it. A route that calls next() lets the request fall through to layers registered below it, including a static handler or a catch-all. An error handler placed before a route cannot catch that route's errors, because the cursor has already moved past it. Passing control on # next() moves to the next matching layer. It is safe to call from nested callbacks and after an await : js Copy app. use ( async (req, res, next) => { const user = await loadUser (req); req. user = user; next (); }); Two rules keep the stack sane: Call next() once . A nextCalled latch on each layer ignores duplicates. Do not call next() and send a response. If a layer responds, the request is finished; a later next() simply has nothing to do. Errors are the exception you want to forward: js Copy app. use ((req, res, next) => { try { risky (); next (); } catch (err) { next (err); // jump to the error chain } }); Throwing synchronously does the same thing, as does rejecting from an async middleware. routiva attaches .catch(next) to every returned promise, so this works without a wrapper: js Copy app. use ( async (req, res, next) => { await mightFail (); // a rejection becomes next(err) automatically next (); }); Error middleware # A function with four parameters is an error handler. Arity is the only marker — there is no separate registration API: js Copy app. use ((err, req, res, next) => { console. error (err); res. status (err. status || 500 ). json ({ error: { message: err. message } }); }); During normal flow, four-arity functions are skipped; during error flow, three-arity functions are skipped. Register error handlers last . The full story — HttpError , expose stack , the default handler and 404/405 — is on the Error handling page. Mounting a Router # A Router is middleware too. app.use('/prefix', router) mounts a whole sub-stack: js Copy import { App, Router } from 'routiva' ; const users = new Router (); users. get ( '/' , (req, res) => res. json ([])); users. get ( '/:id' , (req, res) => res. json ({ id: req. params . id })); const app = new App (); app. use ( '/users' , users); Because routers are just middleware, they compose: mount one router inside another, or mix router methods with use() on the same prefix. Writing your own # A reusable middleware is a factory that returns the function. Keep the setup in the factory and the per-request work in the returned closure: js Copy export function timing () { return function timingMiddleware (req, res, next) { const start = process. hrtime . bigint (); res. raw . on ( 'finish' , () => { const ms = Number (process. hrtime . bigint () - start) / 1e6 ; res. set ( 'X-Duration-Ms' , ms. toFixed ( 1 )); // no effect once sent console. log ( `${req.method} ${req.url} ${res.statusCode} ${ms.toFixed(1)}ms` ); }); next (); }; } A few practical notes: The factory pattern ( timing() returns a function) lets callers pass options and keeps the built-in middleware consistent. Every built-in follows it. req.raw and res.raw expose the underlying IncomingMessage and ServerResponse for anything the wrappers do not cover. Setting a header after the response has started does nothing — do header work before you call next() . Attaching data to the request # A common pattern is to look something up once and stash it on req for later layers: js Copy app. use ( '/api' , async (req, res, next) => { req. db = await pool. connect (); next (); }); app. get ( '/api/users' , (req, res) => { res. json ( rowsFrom (req. db )); }); A conditional guard # js Copy app. use ( '/admin' , (req, res, next) => { if (req. header ( 'authorization' ) !== `Bearer ${SECRET}` ) { return next ( new HttpError ( 401 , 'unauthorized' )); } next (); }); The built-in middleware # routiva ships the pieces most apps need. Each is documented on its own page: Factory Page json urlencoded text raw Body parsing serveStatic Static fil

title: Request & Response
description: Every field and helper on the wrapped req and res objects, from req.accepts() to res.format() and res.sendFile().
text:
The wrappers # Each request is wrapped once. Node's IncomingMessage becomes a Request and its ServerResponse becomes a Response . Both originals stay reachable, so the wrapper is a convenience layer rather than a cage: js Copy req. raw ; // the IncomingMessage res. raw ; // the ServerResponse Anything the wrapper does not cover ( req.raw.setTimeout() , res.raw.writeHead() , res.raw.socket ) is one property away. Everything the wrapper does cover is listed below. Request # Request parses the URL, query string, cookies and client IP in its constructor, so per-request work happens once, not on every property read. Member Type Notes raw IncomingMessage The underlying stream app App The app handling this request method string 'GET' , 'POST' , … url string Current URL, minus any stripped mount prefix originalUrl string The original URL, unchanged path string Pathname only, no query string search string Query string including ? , or '' query object Parsed query; repeated keys become arrays params object Route parameters, set during dispatch body any Set by body-parser middleware cookies object Parsed Cookie header, j: values decoded headers object Lower-cased header map hostname string Host without the port protocol `'http' \ 'https'` secure boolean X-Forwarded-Proto or a TLS socket ip string Client IP, honouring trust proxy ips string[] Forwarded chain, nearest first js Copy app. get ( '/search' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ path: req. path , // '/search' q: req. query . q , // 'cats' tags: req. query . tag , // ['a', 'b'] for ?tag=a&tag=b ip: req. ip , }); }); Request methods # Method Returns req.header(name) The header value (case-insensitive) or undefined req.get(name) Alias for header() req.accepts(...types) The first accepted type, or false req.is(...types) Whether the request Content-Type matches js Copy req. header ( 'user-agent' ); req. accepts ( 'json' , 'html' ); // 'json' | 'html' | false req. is ( 'json' ); // true for application/json req. is ( 'json' , 'text/*' ); // true for JSON or any text type accepts() with no arguments returns the raw Accept header (defaulting to */* ). is() accepts shorthand names ( 'json' , 'html' ) and media ranges such as 'text/*' . Cookies # The Cookie header is parsed for you. Values written as j: JSON — which is what res.cookie() produces for object values — are decoded back: js Copy app. get ( '/' , (req, res) => { const theme = req. cookies . theme ; // string const prefs = req. cookies . prefs ; // object, if written as j: JSON res. json ({ theme, prefs }); }); Response # Response makes every mutator return this , so calls chain: js Copy res. status ( 201 ). type ( 'json' ). send ({ ok: true }); Member Description res.raw The underlying ServerResponse res.req The matching Request res.locals A per-response object for your own data res.statusCode Get/set the status code res.headersSent true once the response has started res.finished true once the response has ended Setting headers # js Copy res. status ( 200 ); res. set ( 'X-Request-Id' , 'abc' ); // one header res. set ({ 'Cache-Control' : 'no-store' }); // many at once res. header ( 'X-Other' , 'v' ); // alias for set() res. append ( 'Set-Cookie' , 'a=1' ); // append to a multi-value header res. get ( 'Content-Type' ); // read one back res. vary ( 'Accept' ); // add to Vary, de-duplicated vary() merges with any existing Vary value and ignores duplicates. Content type # js Copy res. type ( 'json' ); // application/json; charset=utf-8 res. type ( 'html' ); // text/html; charset=utf-8 res. type ( '.css' ); // text/css; charset=utf-8 res. type ( 'image/png' ); // used verbatim when it contains "/" Sending a body # res.send() picks a behaviour from the value it is given: Body Content-Type Behaviour null / undefined text/plain Empty body, Content-Length: 0 Buffer application/octet-stream Raw bytes object / array application/json Delegates to res.json() string / number text/html Written as UTF-8 A Content-Type is only set when the response does not already have one. res.json(value) sets application/json; charset=utf-8 when needed and serializes with JSON.stringify . js Copy res. json ({ ok: true }); res. send ( '

Hello

' ); res. send (Buffer. from ( 'bytes' )); res. sendStatus ( 204 ); // status + reason phrase as text The write-once guard # res.send() , res.json() and friends check headersSent || writableEnded first. A stray second res.json() is silently ignored instead of crashing with ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT : js Copy app. get ( '/' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ first: true }); res. json ({ second: true }); // no-op }); Cookies # js Copy res. cookie ( 'session' , 'abc123' , { httpOnly: true , secure: true , sameSite: 'lax' , maxAge: 1000 * 60 * 60 , // milliseconds path: '/' , }); res. clearCookie ( 'session' ); // expires it immediately res.cookie() merges into any existing Set-Cookie header rather than overwriting it, so several cookies can be set in one response. Supported options: path , maxAge (ms), expires , domain , secure , httpOnly , sameSite ( true means Strict ) and partitioned . Object values are stored as j: JSON, which req.cookies decodes automatically. Redirects and downloads # js Copy res. redirect ( '/login' ); // 302 res. redirect ( 301 , '/new' ); // explicit status res. sendStatus ( 403 ); // 403 with the reason phrase as body res. attachment ( 'report.csv' ); // Content-Disposition: attachment res. sendFile ( 'reports/q3.pdf' ); // resolves a path from the cwd res. download ( 'reports/q3.pdf' , 'Q3 2026.pdf' ); redirect() accepts both (url, status) and (status, url) . sendFile() and download() share the static-file engine — see Static files for conditional and range requests. Content negotiation # res.format() chooses a handler from the client's Accept header, sets Vary: Accept , and falls back to default or 406 : js Copy app. get ( '/greet' , (req, res) => { res. format ({ json: () => res. json ({ hello: 'world' }), html: () => res. send ( '
