title: Body parsing
description: Parse JSON, form, text and raw request bodies into req.body with size limits and content-type gating.
text: The four parsers # routiva ships four body parsers, all built on one streaming reader: json() for application/json urlencoded() for application/x-www-form-urlencoded text() for text/plain raw() for a Buffer of anything Each one writes a parsed value to req.body and shares the same size-limit and error semantics, so you can stack them and let each parser decide whether the request is its job. js Copy import { App, json, urlencoded, text, raw } from 'routiva' ; const app = new App (); app. use ( json ({ limit: '1mb' })); app. use ( urlencoded ({ extended: true })); app. use ( text ()); app. use ( raw ()); App.json() , App.urlencoded() , App.text() and App.raw() are the same functions attached to the App class. How a parser decides to run # Every parser runs the same three checks before touching the stream: Already parsed? If req.body !== undefined , it calls next() without reading. This is what makes stacking safe — the first parser that handles the request wins and the rest become no-ops. Is there a body? A request has one when transfer-encoding is present, or content-length is present and greater than 0 . A plain GET is skipped. Does the content type match? The request's content-type is compared to the parser's expected type with a case-insensitive substring match, so application/json; charset=utf-8 matches application/json . If any check fails the parser calls next() and leaves req.body as undefined . Gating is a substring match, not a media-type parse. application/vnd.api+json does not contain the string application/json , so the default json() parser skips it. Pass { type: 'application/vnd.api+json' } , or use text() / raw() for those. json() # js Copy app. post ( '/users' , json ({ limit: '100kb' }), (req, res) => { res. status ( 201 ). json (req. body ); }); Option Default Behaviour limit '1mb' Maximum body size; overflow rejects with 413 type 'application/json' Content-Type substring to match strict true Body must start with { or [ reviver undefined Passed straight to JSON.parse verify undefined Called as verify(req, res, buffer, 'utf-8') before parsing Behaviour worth knowing: An empty body sets req.body = {} instead of leaving it undefined . With the default strict: true , a bare 42 , "hello" or true is rejected before parsing. Set strict: false to accept any valid JSON value. Malformed JSON rejects with an HttpError(400) whose type is entity.parse.failed and whose body property holds the raw text. Oversized bodies reject with an HttpError(413) with type: 'entity.too.large' and the message Request entity too large . verify runs after the strict check and before JSON.parse . Because it runs inside the read promise, throwing from verify routes into your error middleware — exactly what a webhook signature check needs. verify and webhook signatures # verify gets the raw buffer, so it can validate a signature over the exact bytes the client sent, before any JSON transformation: js Copy import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto' ; import { HttpError, json } from 'routiva' ; app. post ( '/webhooks/stripe' , json ({ verify (req, res, buffer) { const expected = createHmac ( 'sha256' , SECRET). update (buffer). digest ( 'hex' ); const received = req. header ( 'x-signature' ) || '' ; const a = Buffer. from (expected); const b = Buffer. from (received); if (a. length !== b. length || ! timingSafeEqual (a, b)) { throw new HttpError ( 400 , 'invalid signature' , { type: 'signature.invalid' }); } }, }), (req, res) => { res. json ({ received: true }); }); urlencoded() # js Copy app. use ( urlencoded ({ extended: true })); Option Default Behaviour limit '100kb' Maximum body size extended false Decode bracket notation into nested objects urlencoded() has no type option — it always matches application/x-www-form-urlencoded . The body is read with URLSearchParams , so + and percent-escapes are decoded for you. With the default extended: false , keys stay flat and the last value wins: text Copy name=ada&role=admin&role=user -> { name: 'ada', role: 'user' } With extended: true , bracket notation builds nested objects: text Copy user[name]=ada&user[address][city]=london -> { user: { name: 'ada', address: { city: 'london' } } } The extended parser builds objects only . Array notation such as tags[]=a&tags[]=b stores a key literally named '' , not an array. Send JSON when you need arrays. text() # js Copy app. post ( '/notes' , text ({ type: 'text/plain' }), (req, res) => { res. json ({ length: req. body . length }); }); Option Default Behaviour limit '100kb' Maximum body size type 'text/plain' Content-Type substring to match encoding 'utf8' Passed to buffer.toString(encoding) req.body is a string. Pass a broader type to accept other text-ish content types. raw() # js Copy app. post ( '/upload' , raw ({ type: 'application/octet-stream' , limit: '5mb' }), (req, res) => { res. json ({ bytes: req. body . length }); }); Option Default Behaviour limit '100kb' Maximum body size type unset When omitted, every content type is accepted; when set, it must match req.body is a Buffer . Unlike the other three parsers, raw() does not gate on content type unless you pass type , which makes it the catch-all parser to register last. Size limits # Limits are parsed by parseBytes , which understands bare numbers and unit suffixes: Value Bytes 1024 1,024 '100kb' 102,400 '1mb' 1,048,576 '2gb' 2,147,483,648 When the accumulated size exceeds the limit, the reader stops collecting chunks, drains the rest of the stream with stream.resume() so the socket stays writable, and rejects with a 413 . An unparsable limit falls back to that parser's default. What the client sees # Body-parser errors are HttpError s, so the default error handler renders them as JSON: Situation Status type Default message Malformed JSON 400 entity.parse.failed the JSON.parse error message Non-object/array under strict 400 entity.parse.failed JSON body must be an object or array Body over limit 413 entity.too.large Request entity too large Be

title: Static files
description: Serve a directory with serveStatic, and send individual files with res.sendFile, res.download and res.attachment.
text: serveStatic(root, options) # serveStatic() is middleware. It resolves each request path inside root and, when it finds a file, streams it with the correct headers. When it doesn't, it hands control to the next layer. js Copy import { App, serveStatic } from 'routiva' ; const app = new App (); app. use ( serveStatic ( 'public' , { maxAge: '1h' })); App.serveStatic() and the App.static alias point at the same function. Options # Option Default Behaviour fallthrough true Misses call next() ; set false to answer missing files with 404 dotfiles 'ignore' 'ignore' skips, 'deny' returns 403 , 'allow' serves them index ['index.html'] Files tried when the path resolves to a directory; false disables indexing extensions [] Extensions appended when the exact path is not a file redirect true Redirect directory requests instead of resolving them maxAge 0 Sets Cache-Control: public, max-age=… ; 0 emits no cache header immutable false Appends immutable to Cache-Control when maxAge is set etag true Emit a weak ETag ; false disables it headers unset Object of extra headers set on every response type unset Overrides the Content-Type derived from the file extension redirect defaults to true , but the current findFile never produces a redirect target, so a directory with no matching index falls through (or 404 s) rather than redirecting. A directory is only served through its index list. What it handles # Methods. Only GET and HEAD . Every other method calls next() immediately, so it composes with POST routes on the same path. Traversal. The path is percent-decoded, normalised and joined to root , then verified to stay inside it. ..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd resolves outside the root and is rejected. A NUL byte is rejected too. Dotfiles. Files or directories whose name starts with . follow the dotfiles policy. 'ignore' is the safe default. Index files. A request for a directory walks the index list in order and serves the first match that is a regular file. Extension fallback. If the exact path is neither a file nor a directory, each entry of extensions is tried in order. Fallthrough. If nothing is found, next() runs unless fallthrough is false , in which case the middleware raises HttpError(404) . Path resolution # resolveWithin(root, requestPath, dotfiles) returns an absolute path, null to skip, or 'deny' : Request path Result /style.css <root>/style.css /..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd null (escapes root) /a/%00b null (NUL byte) /.env with dotfiles: 'ignore' null /.env with dotfiles: 'deny' 'deny' → 403 /.env with dotfiles: 'allow' <root>/.env Index and extension examples # js Copy // Serve public/index.html for "/", public/index.htm as a fallback. app. use ( serveStatic ( 'public' , { index: [ 'index.html' , 'index.htm' ] })); // Disable directory indexes entirely. app. use ( serveStatic ( 'public' , { index: false })); // GET /about serves public/about.html. app. use ( serveStatic ( 'public' , { extensions: [ 'html' ] })); Extension fallback runs only after the exact path and directory index checks fail, so it never shadows a real file. Conditional and range requests # File responses are handled by send.js , the same engine res.sendFile() uses. For every file it sets Last-Modified , Accept-Ranges: bytes and a weak ETag of the form W/"<size-hex>-<mtime-hex>" . text Copy stat file │ ├─ If-None-Match / If-Modified-Since still fresh ─▶ 304 (no body) ├─ Range: bytes=a-b ─▶ 206 + Content-Range, stream the slice ├─ bad range ─▶ 416 + Content-Range: bytes */size └─ else ─▶ 200 + Content-Length, stream the file Matching rules: If-None-Match: * is always fresh. Otherwise the header is split on commas and each tag is compared for exact equality with the ETag. With etag: false the check is skipped. If-Modified-Since is compared at whole-second resolution, because HTTP dates carry no milliseconds. A range request must match bytes=<start>-<end> exactly. Multiple ranges in one header are not supported — an unrecognised value is treated as no range. Valid forms: Header Meaning bytes=0-499 First 500 bytes bytes=500- From byte 500 to the end bytes=-500 Last 500 bytes bytes=0-0 A single byte A suffix of 0 , or a start beyond the file size, is answered with 416 . Caching # maxAge is parsed by parseDuration , which accepts numbers or strings like '500ms' , '30s' , '10m' , '1h' , '7d' . js Copy // Hashed assets: cache for a year, safe because the name changes on edit. // Note the largest duration unit is weeks, so a year is expressed as 365d. app. use ( '/assets' , serveStatic ( 'public/assets' , { maxAge: '365d' , immutable: true })); // HTML: revalidate on every request. app. use ( serveStatic ( 'public' , { etag: true , maxAge: 0 })); Only when maxAge is greater than zero is Cache-Control: public, max-age=… sent, with , immutable appended when requested. With the default maxAge: 0 no Cache-Control header is written, so clients fall back to the ETag and Last-Modified revalidation above. res.sendFile() and res.download() # Single-file responses reuse the same engine: js Copy app. get ( '/report' , (req, res) => { res. sendFile ( 'reports/q3.pdf' ); // inline }); app. get ( '/report/download' , (req, res) => { res. download ( 'reports/q3.pdf' , 'Q3 2026.pdf' ); }); res.sendFile(filePath, options?, callback?) resolves the path against the process working directory and accepts the same maxAge , etag , headers and type options as serveStatic() . It returns a promise; if you pass a callback it returns this . A missing file rejects with HttpError(404) , so it flows into your error middleware. res.download(filePath, filename?, options?, callback?) is sendFile plus a Content-Disposition: attachment header. Arguments shift: a function filename is treated as the callback, and an object filename is treated as options . res.attachment(filename?) sets Content-Disposition: attachment on its own. Non-ASCII names get an RFC 5987 filename*=UTF-8''… parameter alongside a sanitised ASCII filename . MIME types # lookupMime(filePath) maps an extension to a ty

title: Error handling
description: Route errors into 4-argument middleware, throw HttpError, and understand the default JSON error and 404/405 responses.
text: next(err) is the switch # Handlers either finish the response or call next() . Calling next(err) with a truthy value switches the stack into error mode: from that point, only 4-argument error handlers are eligible. js Copy app. get ( '/users/:id' , (req, res, next) => { const user = users. get (req. params . id ); if (!user) return next ( new HttpError ( 404 , 'user not found' )); res. json (user); }); Two things reach error middleware automatically, with no wrapper library: A synchronous throw inside any handler. A rejected promise returned by any handler. The router calls .catch(next) on every returned promise. js Copy app. get ( '/data' , async (req, res) => { const row = await db. get (req. params . id ); // rejection → error middleware res. json (row); }); Express 4 only forwarded synchronous throws; routiva forwards both. Error middleware # An error handler is any function whose length === 4 . There is no registration API — arity is the marker. js Copy app. use ((err, req, res, next) => { console. error (err); res. status (err. status || 500 ). json ({ error: { message: err. message } }); }); The dispatch loop skips 4-arity functions during normal flow and skips 3-arity functions during error flow, so the same stack serves both. Ordering matters, exactly as with regular middleware: Register error handlers after the routes whose errors they should catch. Registering one before a route means that route's errors will not reach it, because the cursor has already moved past it. Inside an error handler you can: Send a response, ending the chain. Call next(err) to pass the error to the next error handler (for example WARN, then a final JSON handler). Call next() with no argument to drop back into normal flow at the current cursor. Call next after the response is sent — the response is write-once, so extra calls are ignored. HttpError # HttpError carries an HTTP status and marks itself safe to expose: js Copy import { HttpError } from 'routiva' ; throw new HttpError ( 422 , 'validation failed' , { type: 'validation.failed' }); Argument Type Notes status number Also assigned to statusCode message string Defaults to the status reason phrase options.expose boolean Overrides the default exposure of the message options.type string Machine-readable error code, echoed in the response options.cause Error Underlying error, kept off the wire error.expose is set to status < 500 || options.expose === true . In other words, 4xx messages are safe to send and 5xx messages are hidden unless you opt in. The constructor also preserves a cause and sets the error name to HttpError . Convenience constructors: Call Status HttpError.badRequest(message?, options?) 400 HttpError.unauthorized(message?, options?) 401 HttpError.forbidden(message?, options?) 403 HttpError.notFound(message?, options?) 404 HttpError.methodNotAllowed(message?, options?) 405 HttpError.tooLarge(message?, options?) 413 HttpError.internal(message?, options?) 500 The default error handler # If no error middleware sends a response, App._handleError runs. It normalises the error first: it accepts anything ( next('oops') becomes new Error('oops') ), reads err.status or err.statusCode , and uses it only when it is an integer between 400 and 599 . Everything else becomes 500 . The body is JSON: json Copy { "error" : { "message" : "user not found" , "status" : 404 , "type" : "validation.failed" } } type is included only when error.type is set. stack is included only when the expose stack setting is on and the status is >= 500 and a stack exists. message is error.message when the error is exposed or expose stack is on; otherwise it is the canonical reason phrase for the status. expose stack and production # The expose stack setting defaults to env !== 'production' , where env comes from options.env , then NODE_ENV , then 'development' . So in development the real message and a 5xx stack are returned; with NODE_ENV=production a 500 returns { "error": { "message": "Internal Server Error", "status": 500 } } with no stack. Error expose Development Production HttpError(404, 'user not found') true user not found user not found HttpError(500, 'db down') false db down + stack Internal Server Error new Error('boom') unset boom + stack Internal Server Error Set it explicitly with app.set('expose stack', true/false) or the exposeStack constructor option. For a single error, set options.expose: true on the HttpError . Headers already sent # If a handler throws after it has started writing, the response cannot be replaced. The default handler checks res.raw.headersSent and, rather than crashing with ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT , aborts the socket with res.raw.destroy() . Your own error middleware should make the same check: js Copy app. use ((err, req, res, next) => { if (res. raw . headersSent ) return next (err); // let the default handler abort res. status ( 500 ). json ({ error: { message: 'Internal Server Error' , status: 500 } }); }); 404, 405 and OPTIONS # When the stack is exhausted without an error, _handleNotFound runs. If any route matched the path but not the method, that method is recorded and the response describes what is allowed. Situation Response No path matched 404 + { error: { message: 'Not Found', status: 404, path: req.originalUrl } } Path matched, wrong method 405 + Allow header + { error: { message: 'Method Not Allowed', status: 405 } } OPTIONS on a known path 204 + Allow header, empty body The Allow list is sorted and always includes OPTIONS . When a GET route exists, HEAD is recorded alongside it, so a GET -only path reports Allow: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS . This is stricter than Express, which returns 404 for a wrong method, and matches RFC 9110. Customising # Add your own error middleware after the routes. A typical handler logs, then renders a stable shape: js Copy import { App, HttpError } from 'routiva' ; const app = new App (); app. get ( '/users/:id' , (req, res) => { throw new HttpError ( 404 , 'user not found' , { type: 'user.not_found' })

title: CORS
description: Cross-origin headers, automatic preflight handling and an allow-list origin function for production.
text: What cors() does # cors() sets the Access-Control-* headers a browser needs for a cross-origin request, and answers OPTIONS preflight requests for you. js Copy import { createApp, cors } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); app. use ( cors ({ origin: 'https://example.com' , credentials: true })); Register it once, before your routes, and it runs on every request that reaches it. It never ends the request except during a preflight. Options # Option Default Meaning origin '*' Allowed origin: string, array, true (reflect), '*' , or a function methods 'GET,HEAD,PUT,PATCH,POST,DELETE' Value for Access-Control-Allow-Methods credentials false Also send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true preflightContinue false Call next() after a preflight instead of responding optionsSuccessStatus 204 Status code used for the automatic preflight response maxAge undefined Access-Control-Max-Age in seconds; header is omitted when unset allowedHeaders reflect request Value for Access-Control-Allow-Headers exposedHeaders undefined Value for Access-Control-Expose-Headers methods , allowedHeaders and exposedHeaders accept either a string or an array. Arrays are joined with , (no space) when written to the header. Resolving origin # origin accepts several shapes. The resolution lives in resolveOrigin : origin value Behaviour '*' (default) Sends * , unless credentials is true — then it reflects the request Origin true Reflects the request Origin (falls back to * when the request has none) 'https://example.com' Sends that exact string for every request ['https://a.com', 'https://b.com'] Reflects the request Origin only when it is in the array `(origin, req) => string \ false` The request origin comes from the Origin header. When an array value does not contain it, or a function returns false , the middleware sets no CORS headers at all and simply calls next() . A literal Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is invalid together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true . routiva handles this for you: with the default '*' and credentials: true , it reflects the request Origin instead. Which headers are set # For any non-preflight request where an origin resolves to a truthy value: Access-Control-Allow-Origin — the resolved origin. Vary: Origin — only when the resolved origin is not * . Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true — when credentials is set. Access-Control-Expose-Headers — when exposedHeaders is set. For OPTIONS requests, additionally: Access-Control-Allow-Methods — always, from methods . Access-Control-Allow-Headers — only when allowedHeaders is set, or the request already sent Access-Control-Request-Headers (which is echoed). Access-Control-Max-Age — only when maxAge != null . Then control continues to next() . How preflight is answered # An OPTIONS request is treated as a preflight whenever it reaches the middleware. The flow is: text Copy OPTIONS /api/items │ ├─ resolve origin from `Origin` ├─ set ACAO / Vary / credentials / expose headers ├─ set Access-Control-Allow-Methods ├─ echo Access-Control-Request-Headers (or use allowedHeaders) ├─ set Access-Control-Max-Age (when maxAge is set) │ └─ preflightContinue? ├─ true → next() (headers stay set; your route owns the response) └─ false → 204 (optionsSuccessStatus) + empty body With the default preflightContinue: false , the middleware ends the request with res.status(optionsSuccessStatus).send() — a 204 with Content-Length: 0 . Set preflightContinue: true when you want a route or another middleware to produce the OPTIONS response; the CORS headers are already on the response by then. Because cors() answers OPTIONS itself, it takes precedence over routiva's built-in automatic OPTIONS handling. A production allow-list # Use a function to enforce an allow-list and reflect only the origins you trust. Mixing credentials: true with a reflected origin is the correct combination. js Copy import { createApp, cors } from 'routiva' ; const ALLOWED = new Set ([ 'https://app.example.com' , 'https://admin.example.com' , ]); const app = createApp (); app. use ( cors ({ origin (origin, req) { // No Origin header: not a browser cross-origin request. if (!origin) return false ; return ALLOWED. has (origin) ? origin : false ; }, credentials: true , methods: [ 'GET' , 'POST' , 'PATCH' , 'DELETE' ], allowedHeaders: [ 'Content-Type' , 'Authorization' ], exposedHeaders: [ 'X-Request-Id' ], maxAge: 86400 , }), ); Returning the request origin (instead of '*' ) is what lets cookies flow. Returning false for an unknown origin leaves the response without CORS headers, so the browser blocks the call. Caching and Vary # Vary: Origin is added whenever the resolved origin is not * , so shared caches key on the request Origin and do not serve one caller's allow-header to another. For a static '*' origin with no credentials, the header is omitted and the response is safe to share. If you serve different origins from the same route, always use a string, function or array — never a bare '*' combined with credentials.

title: Compression
description: gzip, deflate and brotli compression for buffered responses with a size threshold and content-type filter.
text: What compress() does # compress() wraps res.send() and, when the client asks for it, compresses the fully buffered response with node:zlib . It handles the negotiation headers and sets Content-Encoding , Content-Length and Vary for you. js Copy import { createApp, compress, serveStatic } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); app. use ( compress ({ threshold: '1kb' })); app. use ( serveStatic ( 'public' )); Register it early, before the routes or middleware that build responses, so res.send is wrapped in time. Options # Option Default Meaning threshold '1kb' Minimum body size to compress; number or string ( '1kb' , '100kb' ) filter () => true (req, res) => boolean ; return false to skip this request level undefined zlib compression level, passed to gzip and deflate only threshold is parsed with parseBytes , so '1kb' means 1024 bytes. Bodies whose length is less than the threshold are sent uncompressed; a body exactly at the threshold is compressed. filter runs once per request, before any response body exists. level is applied to gzip and deflate. Brotli is called with {} and ignores it, so compress({ level: 9 }) has no effect when the chosen encoding is br . Choosing an encoding # The encoding is picked from the Accept-Encoding request header in a fixed preference order. Quality values ( q= ) are not parsed — the first token that matches wins. Accept-Encoding contains Chosen encoding br br (brotli) gzip (and no br ) gzip deflate (and no br / gzip ) deflate * (none of the above) gzip nothing usable ( identity , empty, absent) none — response is sent as-is The match is on whole tokens, via a word-boundary regex, so x-gzip does not trigger gzip. What gets compressed # The middleware only touches responses that pass every one of these checks: The request method is not HEAD . HEAD is skipped at the top of the middleware. filter(req, res) returns truthy. An encoding was selected from Accept-Encoding . The response has not already started ( headersSent is false). The response has no Content-Encoding yet, and its Cache-Control does not contain no-transform . The body is a string , number or Buffer . null , undefined and plain objects are passed straight through ( objects delegate to res.json ). If a Content-Type is set, it matches the compressible list below. The buffered body is at least threshold bytes. All types in this list are compressed: Type Example text/* text/html , text/plain , text/css application/json JSON responses application/javascript res.type('js') application/xml XML application/xhtml+xml XHTML application/manifest+json Web app manifests image/svg+xml SVG image/png , application/octet-stream and anything else are left untouched. Note that res.send() always assigns a Content-Type (defaulting to text/html ), so in practice most responses have a type to test. Buffered only # Compression happens inside a wrapped res.send , after the body has been built. That makes it a good fit for res.json() , res.send(string) and buffers — and the wrong tool for streams. res.sendFile() and serveStatic() stream from disk. They never call res.send , so those responses pass through uncompressed and keep streaming. res.end(chunk) / res.write(chunk) called directly are not compressed. res.send() on a Buffer is compressed if its Content-Type is compressible. When compression does run, routiva sets Content-Encoding , sets Content-Length to the compressed size, adds Vary: Accept-Encoding , and writes the compressed bytes straight to res.raw.end() . Vary: Accept-Encoding is only added when a response is actually compressed. Responses that skip compression do not get it. Examples # Compress everything that is at least 1kb, and skip small health checks: js Copy app. use ( compress ({ threshold: '1kb' , filter: (req, res) => req. path !== '/health' , }), ); Compress only JSON and text, with a lower threshold: js Copy app. use ( compress ({ threshold: 512 , level: 6 , filter: (req, res) => req. is ( 'json' , 'text/*' ), }), ); A request that compresses, end to end: http Copy GET /report HTTP/1.1 Accept-Encoding : gzip, deflate, br http Copy HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type : application/json; charset=utf-8 Content-Encoding : br Content-Length : 1043 Vary : Accept-Encoding Because the Content-Length now describes the compressed bytes, clients must decompress before reading the body. Node's fetch and most HTTP clients do this automatically. To inspect raw bytes in a test, use the low-level http module, which leaves the body compressed.

title: Rate limiting
description: Fixed-window rate limiting keyed by client IP, with X-RateLimit headers, 429 responses and a pluggable store.
text: What rateLimit() does # rateLimit() counts requests per client in a fixed time window and rejects callers who exceed the limit with a 429 . It sets the standard X-RateLimit-* headers and a Retry-After header on the rejection. js Copy import { createApp, rateLimit } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); app. use ( rateLimit ({ windowMs: 60_000 , max: 100 })); Options # Option Default Meaning windowMs 60000 Window length in milliseconds max 100 Maximum requests per window (alias: limit ) statusCode 429 Status code of the default rejection message 'Too Many Requests' Message in the default JSON rejection headers true Emit X-RateLimit-* and Retry-After (set false to disable) skip () => false (req, res) => boolean ; return true to bypass counting keyGenerator client IP (req, res) => string ; the counter key handler undefined (req, res, next, record) => void for custom rejections store new MemoryStore(windowMs) Counter backend implementing hit(key) The algorithm # The default store uses a fixed window per key. Every request increments the counter; the window resets after windowMs . text Copy hit(key) │ ├─ no record, or record.resetTime <= now? │ record = { count: 0, resetTime: now + windowMs } │ ├─ record.count += 1 └─ return { count, resetTime } limiter(req, res, next) │ ├─ skip(req, res)? ─▶ next() ├─ record = store.hit(keyGenerator(req, res)) ├─ remaining = max(0, max - record.count) ├─ over limit? record.count > max │ ├─ set Retry-After, call handler(...) or send statusCode JSON │ └─ stop └─ next() The count is incremented before it is checked, so with max: 100 the 101st request in a window receives the 429 . A fixed window is cheap but allows a burst at a boundary: a client can send max requests just before the reset and another max just after. For smooth limits, keep the interface and swap in a sliding-window store . Response headers # When headers is true (the default), every request through the limiter gets: Header Value X-RateLimit-Limit max X-RateLimit-Remaining max(0, max - count) X-RateLimit-Reset Window reset time in Unix seconds ( Math.ceil(resetTime / 1000) ) Retry-After Seconds until reset, at least 1 — only on the 429 response Set headers: false to suppress all of them, including Retry-After . The default rejection is JSON, using statusCode and message : json Copy { "error" : { "message" : "Too Many Requests" , "status" : 429 } } The MemoryStore # MemoryStore is a Map -backed fixed-window store exported from the package. js Copy import { rateLimit, MemoryStore } from 'routiva' ; const store = new MemoryStore ( 60_000 ); app. use ( rateLimit ({ store })); Member Description new MemoryStore(windowMs = 60000) Create the store; starts an unref() 'd cleanup timer hit(key) Increment and return { count, resetTime } (resets expired windows) reset(key) Delete one key; with no argument, clear the whole store clearExpired() Drop every record whose resetTime has passed size Number of live keys stop() Stop the background cleanup timer The cleanup timer is unref() 'd, so it never keeps the process alive. Custom stores # The middleware only calls one method: store.hit(key) , which must return { count, resetTime } synchronously . reset , clearExpired and size are conveniences on MemoryStore — the limiter does not use them. js Copy class RedisStore { constructor (windowMs) { this . windowMs = windowMs; } // Must be synchronous: the middleware reads the record on the same tick. hit (key) { const count = redis. incr (key); // node_redis in sync-ish wrapper if (count === 1 ) redis. pexpire (key, this . windowMs ); const ttl = redis. pttl (key); return { count, resetTime: Date. now () + ttl }; } } Most real backends are async, but hit must stay synchronous. Do the async lookup in an earlier middleware, stash a { count, resetTime } on the request, and read it back from key inside hit . Per-route limits # A limiter is ordinary middleware, so attach it to one route and clamp sensitive routes harder than the global default. js Copy import { createApp, rateLimit } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); const loginLimiter = rateLimit ({ windowMs: 15 * 60_000 , max: 10 , message: 'Too many login attempts. Try again later.' , keyGenerator: (req) => `${req.ip}:${req.body?.email ?? ''}` , }); app. post ( '/login' , loginLimiter, async (req, res) => { // ... res. json ({ ok: true }); }); A custom handler takes over the response completely. record carries the current { count, resetTime } : js Copy app. use ( rateLimit ({ max: 20 , handler (req, res, next, record) { res. status ( 429 ). json ({ error: 'rate_limited' , retryAfter: Math. ceil ((record. resetTime - Date. now ()) / 1000 ), }); }, }), ); To disable limiting during tests, pass skip : js Copy app. use ( rateLimit ({ skip: () => process. env . NODE_ENV === 'test' })); How keys are chosen # The default keyGenerator returns req.ip , falling back to req.raw.socket.remoteAddress , then 'unknown' . req.ip respects the app's trust proxy setting: with it off, it is the socket's remoteAddress ; with it on, it comes from X-Forwarded-For (a number selects that many hops from the right). Behind a proxy, enable trust proxy or every caller shares the proxy's IP and the limit. The default store lives in memory, so it counts per process. Multiple instances behind a load balancer each keep their own counters unless you supply a shared store .

title: Logging
description: One log line per request with method, URL, status and duration, and a custom format hook for JSON logs.
text: What logger() does # logger() writes one line per request after the response finishes. The default line includes the time, method, URL, status code and duration. Pass format to emit your own shape. js Copy import { createApp, logger } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); app. use ( logger ()); Register it first so it wraps every request, including ones that end in an error handler. Options # Option Default Meaning stream process.stdout Anything with a .write(string) method format undefined (req, res, ms) => string ; replaces the default line enabled true Set false to disable logging entirely color stream.isTTY Colorize the status code; defaults to on for a TTY When format is undefined , the built-in formatter is used. color defaults to Boolean(stream.isTTY) , so piping to a file turns color off automatically. Force it with color: true or color: false . When the line is written # The middleware starts a process.hrtime.bigint() timer on entry and registers onFinish on both finish and close of res.raw . Logging happens on whichever fires first, and a logged latch guarantees exactly one line per request. Because it runs after the response, res.statusCode and the duration are final — even for responses produced by an error handler downstream. The line is written with stream.write( ${line}\n ) , so a custom format should return a string without a trailing newline. The default format # defaultFormat produces a single space-separated line: text Copy <ISO timestamp> <METHOD> <URL> <STATUS> <ms>ms with the status colorized when useColor is true. The URL is req.originalUrl || req.url , so a mounted router still logs the full path. The duration is ms.toFixed(1) , one decimal place. text Copy 2026-10-14T09:31:02.114Z GET /health 200 3.2ms Status colors are chosen by range: Status Color 5xx red ( 31 ) 4xx yellow ( 33 ) 3xx cyan ( 36 ) otherwise green ( 32 ) The escape codes are only emitted when useColor is true, so redirected output stays clean and copy-pasteable. Custom format # format receives (req, res, ms) , where ms is a number. Return the line you want. This JSON example is suitable for production log pipelines: js Copy import { createApp, logger } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); app. use ( logger ({ format: (req, res, ms) => JSON. stringify ({ time: new Date (). toISOString (), method: req. method , url: req. originalUrl , status: res. statusCode , durationMs: Math. round (ms * 10 ) / 10 , ip: req. ip , }), }), ); Each request writes one compact JSON object: text Copy {"time":"2026-10-14T09:31:02.114Z","method":"POST","url":"/api/orders","status":201,"durationMs":12.4,"ip":"203.0.113.7"} Send logs somewhere other than stdout by passing a writable stream: js Copy import fs from 'node:fs' ; import { logger } from 'routiva' ; const access = fs. createWriteStream ( 'access.log' , { flags: 'a' }); app. use ( logger ({ stream: access, color: false })); Any object with a write(string) method works. A file stream is not a TTY, so color is already off; color: false makes that explicit. Turning it off # enabled: false makes the middleware a no-op — useful when a test harness or an outer logger already covers requests. js Copy app. use ( logger ({ enabled: process. env . NODE_ENV !== 'test' })); Unlike the other built-in middleware, logger() never changes the response: it reads the request and response but sets no headers and writes no body.

title: Examples
description: A runnable demo, a complete CRUD API with a browser UI, and focused snippets for routing, errors, uploads, SPA fallbacks and custom middleware.
text:
Running the bundled examples # From a clone of the repository: bash Copy npm run example # node examples/basic.js → http://localhost:3000 npm run crud # node crud-app/server.js → http://127.0.0.1:3000 examples/basic.js is a single readable file that touches most of the framework. The CRUD app is a full application with a browser UI, persistent storage and its own test suite. examples/basic.js , line by line # The demo registers the built-in middleware in the recommended order, then a handful of routes. js Copy import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url' ; import { App, Router, HttpError } from '../src/index.js' ; const publicDir = fileURLToPath ( new URL ( './public' , import . meta . url )); const app = new App (); // --- Global middleware ----------------------------------------------------- app. use (App. logger ()); app. use (App. cors ({ origin: true , credentials: true })); app. use (App. compress ()); app. use (App. rateLimit ({ windowMs: 60_000 , max: 100 })); app. use (App. json ()); // parse JSON bodies (max 1mb) app. use (App. serveStatic (publicDir, { maxAge: '1h' })); Step Why it is in this order logger() Wraps every request so the completion line is always written cors() Answers preflights before any route work compress() Wraps res.send before bodies are produced rateLimit() Rejects abusive callers before real work json() Parses only JSON requests, leaves others alone serveStatic() Last, so explicit routes win and misses fall through Routes use the wrapped req / res directly: js Copy app. get ( '/health' , (req, res) => res. json ({ status: 'ok' , uptime: process. uptime () })); app. get ( '/users/:id' , (req, res) => { res. json ({ id: req. params . id , query: req. query , cookies: req. cookies }); }); app. post ( '/users' , (req, res) => { res. status ( 201 ). json ({ created: req. body }); }); app. get ( '/download' , (req, res) => { res. download ( fileURLToPath ( new URL ( './public/style.css' , import . meta . url )), 'style.css' ); }); Content negotiation picks a representation from the Accept header: js Copy app. get ( '/greet' , (req, res) => res. format ({ json: () => res. json ({ hello: req. query . name || 'world' }), html: () => res. send ( `

Hello ${req.query.name || 'world'}

` ), default : () => res. status ( 406 ). send ( 'Not Acceptable' ), }), ); A sub-router mounted at a prefix: js Copy const api = new Router (); api. get ( '/status' , (req, res) => res. json ({ status: 'ok' })); app. use ( '/api' , api); // GET /api/status And an error handler, registered last: js Copy app. get ( '/boom' , () => { throw new HttpError ( 500 , 'Something went wrong' ); }); app. use ((err, req, res, next) => { res. status (err. status || 500 ). json ({ error: { message: err. message } }); }); The CRUD application # crud-app/ is a small inventory service built entirely on routiva: a REST API, a JSON-backed store, a browser UI, validation and tests. bash Copy npm run crud URL What Browser UI (create / edit / delete / restock / search) JSON API Health check Configuration is through environment variables: Variable Default Purpose PORT 3000 Listening port HOST 127.0.0.1 Listening host DATA_FILE crud-app/data/products.json JSON datastore The app seeds five sample products on first run. The API # Base path /api . Errors share one envelope: json Copy { "error" : { "message" : "Validation failed" , "status" : 422 , "details" : { "name" : "name is required" } } } Method Path Description GET /api/health Liveness + uptime GET /api/stats Counts and total inventory value GET /api/categories Distinct categories GET /api/products List, with query options below POST /api/products Create → 201 + Location GET /api/products/:id Read one → 200 / 404 PUT /api/products/:id Replace → 200 PATCH /api/products/:id Partial update → 200 POST /api/products/:id/restock Add { "amount": n } to stock DELETE /api/products/:id Delete → 204 List query options: search , category , inStock=true|false , sort=created|name|price|stock , order=asc|desc , page , limit (max 100). Try it: bash Copy curl http:// 127.0 . 0.1 : 3000 /api/products curl -X POST http:// 127.0 . 0.1 : 3000 /api/products \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"name":"Webcam","sku":"CAM-1","price":59.99,"stock":4,"category":"peripherals"}' curl -X POST http:// 127.0 . 0.1 : 3000 /api/products/ 1 /restock \ -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"amount":5}' curl -X DELETE -i http:// 127.0 . 0.1 : 3000 /api/products/ 1 How it is wired # crud-app/app.js exports a createApp() factory so tests can build an isolated instance with a temp data file, logging off and a high rate limit: js Copy export async function createApp ({ dataFile, logging, rateLimitMax, seed } = {}) { const store = await new ProductStore (path. resolve (dataFile)). load (); if (seed) await store. seedIfEmpty (SAMPLE_PRODUCTS); const app = new App ({ env: process. env . NODE_ENV || 'development' }); app. use ( logger ({ enabled: logging })); app. use ( cors ({ origin: true , credentials: true })); app. use ( compress ({ threshold: '1kb' })); app. use ( rateLimit ({ windowMs: 60_000 , max: rateLimitMax })); app. use ( json ({ limit: '100kb' })); app. use ( '/api' , productsRouter (store)); app. use ( serveStatic (publicDir, { maxAge: '5m' , extensions: [ 'html' ] })); app. use ((err, req, res, next) => { if (res. headersSent ) return next (err); let status = err. status || err. statusCode || 500 ; if (err. type === 'entity.parse.failed' ) status = 400 ; else if (err. type === 'entity.too.large' ) status = 413 ; res. status (status). json ({ error: { message: err. message , status } }); }); return { app, store }; } crud-app/routes/products.js is a Router mounted at /api . It uses router.param('id', …) to load and validate the product once for every route with an :id : js Copy router. param ( 'id' , (req, res, next, id) => { const numeric = Number (id); if (!Number. isInteger

title: Testing
description: Test routiva apps with node --test and global fetch, bind servers to port 0, and run the CRUD demo suite.
text: No test framework to install # routiva tests itself with the runner that ships with Node: node --test . Test files import test from node:test and assertions from node:assert/strict . There is no mocha, no jest and no supertest to audit. bash Copy npm test # node --test, runs test/ npm run test:watch # node --test --watch node --test discovers test/**/*.test.js and runs each file in its own process. Two suites live in the repo: test/ and crud-app/test/ . Make real requests # Tests start a server and talk to it over HTTP with the global fetch . That exercises the wrappers, the router, the middleware and Node's socket code together, which is where framework bugs actually surface. Bind to port 0 and let the OS pick the port: js Copy const server = app. listen ( 0 ); await once (server, 'listening' ); const base = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}` ; Fixed ports collide between parallel runs; port 0 removes the problem. A small start helper # test/helpers.js wraps the pattern so each file does not repeat it: js Copy import { once } from 'node:events' ; export async function start (app) { const server = app. listen ( 0 ); await once (server, 'listening' ); const { port } = server. address (); return { server, url: `http://127.0.0.1:${port}` , async close () { if (!server. listening ) return ; server. close (); await once (server, 'close' ); }, }; } A full test file # The shape used across the repo: build the app, start it once in before , close it in after , and assert status, headers and body from fetch . js Copy import { test, before, after } from 'node:test' ; import assert from 'node:assert/strict' ; import { createApp, json } from 'routiva' ; let server; let base; before ( async () => { const app = createApp (); app. use ( json ()); app. get ( '/hello' , (req, res) => res. json ({ hello: 'world' })); app. post ( '/echo' , (req, res) => res. status ( 201 ). json (req. body )); app. get ( '/boom' , () => { throw new Error ( 'nope' ); }); app. use ((err, req, res, next) => { res. status ( 500 ). json ({ error: err. message }); }); server = app. listen ( 0 ); await new Promise ((resolve) => server. once ( 'listening' , resolve)); base = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}` ; }); after ( async () => { await new Promise ((resolve) => server. close (resolve)); }); test ( 'GET /hello returns JSON' , async () => { const res = await fetch ( `${base}/hello` ); assert. equal (res. status , 200 ); assert. match (res. headers . get ( 'content-type' ), /application\/json/); assert. deepEqual ( await res. json (), { hello: 'world' }); }); test ( 'POST /echo returns the parsed body' , async () => { const res = await fetch ( `${base}/echo` , { method: 'POST' , headers: { 'content-type' : 'application/json' }, body: JSON. stringify ({ n: 1 }), }); assert. equal (res. status , 201 ); assert. deepEqual ( await res. json (), { n: 1 }); }); test ( 'a thrown error reaches the error middleware' , async () => { const res = await fetch ( `${base}/boom` ); assert. equal (res. status , 500 ); assert. deepEqual ( await res. json (), { error: 'nope' }); }); before and after are exported by node:test and scoped to the file. Assert the things that break # Status first. A wrong status usually means the route did not match, or a middleware swallowed the request. Headers that carry meaning. Allow on a 405 , Location on a 201 , Content-Type on JSON, Content-Encoding on a compressed response. JSON shape, not string form. assert.deepEqual(await res.json(), {...}) survives key ordering and whitespace. Test middleware in isolation # Mount only the middleware under test and assert its observable behaviour. It is faster to write and isolates the failure: js Copy import { test } from 'node:test' ; import assert from 'node:assert/strict' ; import { createApp, cors } from 'routiva' ; import { start } from './helpers.js' ; test ( 'cors reflects the origin when credentials are on' , async (t) => { const app = createApp (); app. use ( cors ({ origin: true , credentials: true })); app. get ( '/' , (req, res) => res. send ( 'ok' )); const s = await start (app); t. after (() => s. close ()); const res = await fetch (s. url , { headers: { origin: 'https://example.com' } }); assert. equal (res. headers . get ( 'access-control-allow-origin' ), 'https://example.com' ); }); t.after() scopes teardown to one test; before and after scope it to the file. Testing the CRUD demo # The demo has its own end-to-end checks: bash Copy npm run crud:test # node --test crud-app/test/crud.test.js npm run crud:smoke # bash crud-app/curl.sh crud-app/test/crud.test.js builds the app with a temporary data file, logging off and a high rate limit, then walks the full lifecycle: create, read, update, restock, validation, duplicate SKU, 405 , delete and on-disk persistence. The same discipline applies to your app: expose it as a factory that takes its configuration, so a test can point it at a temp path and an ephemeral port. crud-app/curl.sh takes a different route. It boots the real server on port 4123 against a throwaway file, drives every endpoint with curl and prints status codes, then cleans up. crud-app/requests.http holds the same calls for the VS Code REST Client or the JetBrains HTTP client. Scripts # Command What it runs npm test node --test , the framework suite npm run test:watch node --test --watch npm run crud:test node --test crud-app/test/crud.test.js npm run crud:smoke bash crud-app/curl.sh npm run crud node crud-app/server.js npm run example node examples/basic.js Tips # Avoid fixed ports. Use listen(0) plus server.address().port . Always close servers. Use t.after or after so a failed assertion cannot leave a socket open and hang the runner. Disable logging in tests. Pass logger({ enabled: false }) or a config flag so the output stays readable. Use a raw http request when fetch hides the truth. fetch decodes compressed bodies automatically, so the compression test uses the request() helper in test/helpers.js to read bytes and header

title: Performance
description: Why routiva stays fast — compiled routes, a linear dispatch scan, streaming I/O — and how to benchmark your own workload.
text: Fast because it is small # routiva does not quote a throughput number, because a number from one machine does not transfer to another. It is quick for a concrete reason: it does little per request. There is no dependency graph to load, no routing table rebuilt on each call, no body buffered that could be streamed, and no compression performed unless the client asked for it. This page describes the cost model so you can reason about your own app, then shows how to measure it. Where the time goes # A request touches four things: Wrap. new Request(raw) parses the URL, query string and cookies once. Dispatch. The layer stack is scanned until a layer matches and responds. Handler. Your code runs. Serialize. res.send() writes headers and a body. The framework owns steps 1, 2 and 4. Step 2 grows with the number of layers, so the design keeps that scan cheap and predictable. Routes compile once # Patterns become a RegExp at registration time, never per request. compile(pattern, end) in src/router.js : text Copy /users/:id -> /^\/users\/([^/]+)\/?$/ keys: ['id'] /files/* -> /^\/files\/(.*)\/?$/ keys: ['wildcard'] /api (mount) -> /^\/api(?=\/|$)/ prefix, not anchored to the end Literal segments are regex-escaped, :name becomes ([^/]+) and * becomes (.*) . The compiled regex and its keys array are stored on the layer and shared by every request. Dispatch only calls layer.regex.exec(req.path) . The dispatch loop is a linear scan # All routing runs through one function with a shared cursor: js Copy function dispatch (stack, req, res, done) { let index = 0 ; let finished = false ; function next (err) { if (finished) return ; const wantsError = Boolean (err); while (index < stack. length ) { const layer = stack[index++]; if (layer. isErrorHandler !== wantsError) continue ; const match = layer. regex . exec (req. path ); if (!match) continue ; // ...method check, then invoke(layer, match, err, req, res, next) break ; } // stack exhausted -> done(err) } next (); } Two properties matter: next() is O(1), not recursive. The cursor never moves backwards, so a chain of next() calls does not re-scan earlier layers or grow the call stack. Error handlers are skipped for free. During normal flow, four-arity layers are filtered out by a single comparison before the regex is even run. Cost is linear in the number of layers that precede the match. Per-request allocation # The only objects created per request are the two wrappers and the small values they hold: new Request(raw) reads raw.url with the URL constructor once, then splits query and cookies into plain objects. new Response(raw, req) stores two references and an empty locals object. During dispatch, invoke() merges params into a fresh object and saves the previous values so a mounted router can restore them on next() . Nothing clones the stack, and no layer is recompiled. Compression costs CPU to save bytes # compress() wraps res.send() and decides per response: text Copy Accept-Encoding: br, gzip -> pick br, else gzip, else deflate body below threshold -> send as-is Content-Type not text-ish -> send as-is already encoded / streamed -> send as-is The trade is explicit: brotli and gzip burn CPU and latency to shrink a body. The default threshold is 1kb , so small responses skip the work entirely. A response the client cannot benefit from (already encoded, an image, a streamed file) is left alone. If compression shows up in a profile, raise threshold , pin level , or gate it with filter(req, res) . Because routiva buffers res.send() before compressing, it never wraps a file stream. That keeps sendFile streaming, but large generated bodies are compressed in memory. Static files are cheap when cached # send.js stats the file, then: sets ETag ( W/"size-mtime" ) and Last-Modified ; returns 304 immediately when If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since says the client copy is fresh; sets Cache-Control from maxAge and immutable when configured; serves a single Range as 206 by streaming only that slice. The 304 path is the win: no body, no read of the file contents. Set a long maxAge for immutable assets and let conditional requests do the rest. The stat call itself is a filesystem hit per request; that is the floor for this strategy. The rate limit store is a Map # MemoryStore is a fixed-window counter keyed by IP: hit(key) is one Map lookup and an increment; expired keys are swept by an interval timer created with .unref() , so the timer never keeps the process alive; reset() clears one key or the whole store. There is no external store. Run more than one process and each keeps its own counters, so a shared limit needs a custom store . sendFile streams # pipeFile() uses createReadStream(path, range).pipe(res.raw) , so memory stays flat regardless of file size. finish and error events resolve a promise, so the surrounding await still sees failures. Byte ranges stream the same way. Measuring it # Measure your app on your hardware. autocannon and wrk are both good: bash Copy npm install -g autocannon # start your app in another shell node server.js # 10 connections for 10 seconds autocannon -c 10 -d 10 http:// 127.0 . 0.1 : 3000 /api/products # 50 connections, JSON POST bodies autocannon -c 50 -d 20 -m POST \ -H "content-type=application/json" \ -b '{"name":"widget","sku":"W-1","price":1}' \ http:// 127.0 . 0.1 : 3000 /api/products wrk in the same shape: bash Copy wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s http:// 127.0 . 0.1 : 3000 /health wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s -s post.lua http:// 127.0 . 0.1 : 3000 /api/products Watch the shape, not just requests per second: Signal What it tells you requests per second throughput at a given concurrency latency p99 tail behaviour under load CPU per request headroom left for middleware RSS and heap allocation churn and leaks Compare against a real Express build of the same app on the same machine. Both sit on node:http and run your handlers, so the difference comes from the framework's per-request work, not the socket. Practical tips # Register cheap middleware fir

title: Coming from Express
description: Map an Express app onto routiva: what stays identical, what changes, and where Express still wins.
text: The mental model is unchanged # An app is a router. A router is an ordered list of layers. A layer is a route, a piece of middleware, or an error handler. next() moves a request down the list, and registration order is execution order. None of that changes when you move from Express to routiva. The handler signatures are identical, so most route bodies copy over untouched. A function (req, res, next) is middleware in both. A four-arity function (err, req, res, next) is an error handler in both. API mapping # Express routiva const app = express() const app = createApp() or new App() app.use(fn) app.use(fn) app.use('/api', router) app.use('/api', router) app.get/post/put/patch/delete/head/options identical, plus app.all() express.Router() new Router() express.json() json() or App.json() express.urlencoded({ extended: true }) urlencoded({ extended: true }) express.static('public') serveStatic('public') express.text() / express.raw() text() / raw() req.params , req.query , req.body , req.cookies identical req.get(name) / req.header(name) identical res.status/json/send/redirect/type/set/cookie identical res.sendFile(path) / res.download(path) identical req.accepts() / res.format() identical next(err) identical app.use((err, req, res, next) => {}) identical app.listen(port, cb) identical; returns the http.Server The cors , compression , express-rate-limit , morgan , cookie-parser and serve-static imports disappear. Their equivalents are exported by routiva and used the same way. Same shape, less ceremony # A users endpoint in Express, with the packages it needs: js Copy import express from 'express' ; import cors from 'cors' ; import compression from 'compression' ; const app = express (); app. use ( cors ()); app. use ( compression ()); app. use (express. json ()); app. get ( '/users/:id' , async (req, res, next) => { try { const user = await db. find (req. params . id ); if (!user) return res. status ( 404 ). json ({ error: 'not found' }); res. json (user); } catch (err) { next (err); // Express 4 needs this } }); app. listen ( 3000 ); The routiva version: js Copy import { createApp, cors, compress, json } from 'routiva' ; const app = createApp (); app. use ( cors ()); app. use ( compress ()); app. use ( json ()); app. get ( '/users/:id' , async (req, res) => { const user = await db. find (req. params . id ); // a rejection is forwarded if (!user) return res. status ( 404 ). json ({ error: 'not found' }); res. json (user); }); app. listen ( 3000 ); The route body does not change. The try/catch , the extra imports and the separate packages do. What differs # Async errors are handled for you # Express 4 only forwards synchronous throws to error middleware. A rejected promise inside an async handler hangs the request unless you wrap it. routiva attaches .catch(next) to the value every handler returns, so throw and Promise.reject both reach your error middleware. Express 5 catches async errors too; routiva matches that behaviour. 405 with an Allow header # If a path matches but the method does not, routiva answers 405 Method Not Allowed with a correct Allow header. Express returns 404 . For a path that exists, routiva answers OPTIONS automatically with 204 and the same Allow list, and HEAD reuses the matching GET route with the body suppressed. One response, once # res.send() and res.json() are guarded by res.raw.headersSent and res.raw.writableEnded . A stray second res.json() is a no-op instead of an ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT crash. Body parse errors have stable types # json() rejects a body that is not an object or array with 400 entity.parse.failed , and an oversized body with 413 entity.too.large . The type value is set on the error, so one error handler can map both. No template engine or view system # There is no res.render() , no app.set('view engine', ...) , no views directory, no view cache and no app.locals . If your app renders HTML on the server, keep Express or render it yourself and call res.send() . One minor detail: res.locals exists as an empty object on each response, but nothing in the framework reads it for you. Smaller path syntax # routiva supports :name parameters and a * wildcard. Express also supports optional parameters ( :id? ), inline regex ( :id(\d+) ) and arrays of paths. Port those by validating inside router.param() or the handler. Where Express still wins # Ecosystem. Thousands of mature middlewares, adapters and integrations. Rendering. Any template engine via res.render() . Sessions, flash, auth. Passport and its strategies are Express-shaped. Advanced routing. Optional params, regex params and path arrays. Streaming compression. routiva compresses buffered res.send() output; streamed files pass through untouched. Express's compression wraps the whole response stream. Track record. Express has years of production hardening. routiva is a compact, well-tested implementation. Use Express when the ecosystem is doing real work for you. Use routiva when you want the same mental model inside a core you can read end to end. A migration checklist # Replace express() with createApp() and swap require for an import. Move CORS, compression and rate limiting to routiva's bundled factories. Drop cookie-parser ; req.cookies is already parsed. Replace express.json() with json({ limit: '100kb' }) . Delete the try/catch plus next(err) wrappers around async handlers. Replace res.render() call sites before you start. Run your suite against the new app. Most handler bodies will not have changed.

title: FAQ & roadmap
description: Production readiness, TypeScript, websockets, uploads, Node versions, framework comparisons, the roadmap and contributing.
text:
Is it production-ready? # It is small and tested, and the behaviour it implements is deliberate. It is also new. The honest position: It works. There is a real test suite and a runnable demo app. It has not seen years of hostile traffic the way Express has. It ships no ecosystem, so anything beyond the built-in middleware is yours to write. It is a good fit for internal services, prototypes, edge and embedded targets, and any project that values a zero-dependency core. Evaluate it against your own workload before putting it in front of users; nothing here replaces that judgement. Does it work with TypeScript? # There are no bundled type declarations. routiva ships as plain ESM JavaScript. You have three options: Set "allowJs": true and let TypeScript infer what it can from the source. Write a .d.ts file for the surface you use. Write the server in plain JavaScript. The API is regular: classes, named exports and middleware factories. Nothing relies on dynamic shapes that resist typing, so hand-written declarations are straightforward. Bundled types are on the roadmap. Does it support WebSockets or HTTP/2? # Not directly. routiva builds on node:http , and app.listen() returns the underlying http.Server , so you can attach a WebSocket library to its upgrade event. There is no HTTP/2 support and none is planned for the zero-dependency core. Is there a template engine? # No. There is no res.render() , no view engine setting and no app.locals . You compose HTML in a function and send it: js Copy app. get ( '/' , (req, res) => { res. type ( 'html' ). send ( `

Hello

` ); }); Escape any user input you interpolate yourself. If you need a full template engine, pair routiva with a standalone renderer or choose Express, where res.render() is integrated. How do I handle file uploads? # There is no multipart parser. raw() gives you the request body as a Buffer and text() gives it to you as a string, so a single-part upload can be read directly: js Copy app. post ( '/upload' , raw ({ limit: '5mb' }), (req, res) => { res. json ({ bytes: req. body . length }); }); For multipart/form-data , parse the body yourself or run a standalone parsing step. There is no upload middleware in the box, and adding one would bring in the kind of dependency routiva avoids. raw() still enforces a size limit . Which Node versions are supported? # Node 18 and newer, matching "engines": { "node": ">=18" } . The runtime uses standard Node modules ( node:http , node:fs , node:path , node:zlib , and friends), all present on 18. The test suite relies on global fetch and node:test , which are also 18+. There is no build step, so any current LTS or newer works. How is it different from Fastify, Hono or Koa? # routiva Fastify Hono Koa Runtime dependencies 0 some some some Target Node node:http Node multi-runtime Node Schema validation no built in no no TypeScript types not bundled yes yes community Middleware model one ordered stack hooks and plugins one stack onion Opinion Express-like plugin-first tiny and portable minimal Koa replaces req and res with its own context and uses onion middleware. Fastify adds schemas, plugins and serialization. Hono targets edge runtimes and other platforms. routiva keeps Express's stack and handler signatures and stops there. How do I report a bug or contribute? # Open an issue or a pull request on GitHub: github.com/uditc0derr/routiva . A useful bug report has a minimal reproduction, the Node version and what you expected to happen. There is no CLA. Roadmap # Ideas that fit the architecture without breaking the zero-dependency rule, in no committed order: res.render() with a pluggable engine interface. A streaming-safe compression path that wraps the socket, not just res.send . Signed cookies and a lightweight session() store. A full app.mount() with sub-app semantics. Bundled TypeScript declarations. Coverage reporting in CI. None of these has a date. If one matters to you, say so in an issue. Contributing # Repository: uditc0derr/routiva Package: routiva on npm License: MIT Run npm test before opening a pull request. Keep the dependency count at zero: if a Node built-in can do it, use the built-in. Match the existing file layout and the one-layer-per-handler model. Small, focused changes are easier to review than broad rewrites.

title: Architecture
description: How routiva works under the hood — the layer stack, path compilation, dispatch and restoration, body parsing and file sending.
text: High-level map # text Copy Client │ HTTP request ▼ node:http · http.createServer(handler) │ IncomingMessage + ServerResponse ▼ App._handle(rawReq, rawRes) ├─ wrap: new Request(raw) + new Response(raw, req) └─ this.handle(req, res, done) │ ▼ Router.handle → dispatch(this.stack) ├─ logger() → next() ├─ json() → next() ├─ GET /users/:id → res.json(...) ← responds ├─ POST /users → next() ├─ (err,req,res,next) → only after next(err) └─ serveStatic() → next() │ stack exhausted ▼ done(err) ├─ err → _handleError(err) → 4xx / 5xx JSON └─ none → _handleNotFound() → 404 / 405 / OPTIONS The request enters at _handle , is wrapped, then flows through a single ordered list of layers. Each layer either handles the request, passes control onward with next() , or raises an error with next(err) . When the stack is exhausted, done(err) chooses between an error response and a 404/405/OPTIONS. Module dependency graph # text Copy index.js ─────────────────────────────────────────────── public API + statics │ ├── app.js ──────────▶ router.js ──▶ utils.js │ │ │ ├────────────▶ request.js ──▶ utils.js │ │ │ ├────────────▶ response.js ──▶ send.js ──▶ errors.js, utils.js │ │ └──────▶ errors.js │ └────────────▶ errors.js │ └── middleware/ ├── body-parser.js ──▶ errors.js, utils.js ├── static.js ───────▶ send.js, errors.js ├── cors.js ├── compress.js ─────▶ utils.js, node:zlib ├── logger.js └── rate-limit.js The graph is acyclic and shallow. errors.js and utils.js are leaves; send.js is the only shared low-level utility used by two entry points ( res.sendFile() and serveStatic() ). Module reference # Module Responsibility src/index.js Public entry point; attaches middleware factories as App statics src/app.js App : server lifecycle, settings, default 404/405/error handling src/router.js Router : layer stack, path compilation, dispatch, param / route / use src/request.js Request wrapper: URL, query, cookies, IP, negotiation src/response.js Response wrapper: chainable helpers, cookies, send, sendFile, format src/send.js File sending: MIME lookup, ETag, Last-Modified , Range, streaming src/errors.js HttpError + HTTP reason phrases src/utils.js Query/cookie/accept parsing, byte & duration parsing, regex escaping src/middleware/body-parser.js json() , urlencoded() , text() , raw() src/middleware/static.js serveStatic() with traversal protection and fallthrough src/middleware/cors.js cors() with preflight handling src/middleware/compress.js compress() via gzip / deflate / brotli src/middleware/logger.js logger() request logging src/middleware/rate-limit.js rateLimit() + MemoryStore fixed windows The layer stack # Router holds a single array, this.stack . Registering anything pushes one layer per handler function : js Copy // src/router.js — _register() (abridged) const { regex, keys } = compile (path, !isMiddleware); // compiled once, shared for ( const fn of flat) { const handler = fn instanceof Router ? wrapRouter (fn) : fn; this . stack . push ({ method, // 'GET' | null (middleware / all) path, // original pattern, for debugging regex, // compiled matcher keys, // captured parameter names fn: handler, // the function actually invoked owner: this , // which Router registered it (for param callbacks) isMiddleware, // prefix match vs exact match isErrorHandler: handler. length === 4 , // arity-based classification }); } Because routes and middleware live in the same list, registration order is execution order . A route registered with several handlers pushes several layers that share one compiled regex and keys array. Path matching # Patterns are compiled to a RegExp once, at registration time: text Copy / end → /^\/?$/ prefix → /^/ /users/:id end → /^\/users\/([^/]+)\/?$/ /files/* end → /^\/files\/(.*)\/?$/ /users prefix → /^\/users(?=\/|$)/ Normalise leading/trailing slashes. Split on :name and * tokens, keeping the literals. Regex-escape the literals; :name → ([^/]+) , * → (.*) . end: true anchors with ^…\/?$ — an exact match for routes, tolerating a trailing slash. end: false uses a lookahead ^…(?=\/|$) — a prefix match for mounted middleware, without consuming the next / . The keys array records parameter names in capture order, so invoke() can zip match[1..n] back onto names: js Copy layer. keys . forEach ((key, i) => { const value = match[i + 1 ]; if (value !== undefined ) params[key] = safeDecode (value); // URL-decode captures }); safeDecode wraps decodeURIComponent , so a malformed % never throws a 500. Dispatch and next() # All dispatching lives in one function, dispatch(stack, req, res, done) . It uses a shared cursor ( index ) plus a finished latch, so next() calls from any depth walk the same list without re-running earlier layers: js Copy // src/router.js — dispatch() (abridged) function dispatch (stack, req, res, done) { let index = 0 ; let finished = false ; function next (err) { if (finished) return ; // one terminal transition only if (index >= stack. length ) { finished = true ; return done (err); // stack exhausted } const wantsError = Boolean (err); let layer, match; while (index < stack. length ) { layer = stack[index++]; if (layer. isErrorHandler !== wantsError) continue ; // error ⇔ 4-arity only match = layer. regex . exec (req. path ); if (!match) continue ; if (! methodAllows (layer, req)) { // HEAD→GET fallback if (!layer. isMiddleware ) recordAllowed (req, layer. method ); match = null ; continue ; } break ; } if (!match) { finished = true ; return done (err); } invoke (layer, match, err, req, res, next); } next (); } A while loop keeps stack depth O(1) per next() call and guarantees the cursor never moves backwards. finished ensures done runs exactly once even if a handler calls next() repeatedly. methodAllows lets a HEAD request use a GET route. When a path matches but the method does not, recordAllowed notes the method (and HEAD for GET ) so _handleNotFound can build the Allow header. Params, mount prefixes and restoration # invoke() runs a layer and does four careful things: 1. Build and mer
